```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

## Summary

The goal is to predict the `classe` variable (A to E), which describes how a participant performed a barbell lift, using accelerometer data from the belt, forearm, arm and dumbbell. A is the correct form, and B to E are four common mistakes. I trained a random forest with 5-fold cross-validation, held out 30% of the training data to estimate out-of-sample error, and used the final model to predict the 20 test cases.

Data source: Velloso, E., Bulling, A., Gellersen, H., Ugulino, W., Fuks, H. *Qualitative Activity Recognition of Weight Lifting Exercises.* Proceedings of the 4th Augmented Human International Conference, 2013. http://groupware.les.inf.puc-rio.br/har

## Loading and cleaning the data

```{r load}
library(caret)
library(randomForest)

train_url <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-training.csv"
test_url  <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/predmachlearn/pml-testing.csv"

training <- read.csv(train_url, na.strings = c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!"))
testing  <- read.csv(test_url,  na.strings = c("NA", "", "#DIV/0!"))
dim(training)
```

Cleaning steps and why:

1. **Dropped the first 7 columns** (row index, user name, timestamps, window info). They are identifiers, not sensor measurements, and would let the model "cheat" on this dataset without generalizing.
2. **Dropped columns that are mostly NA** (more than 90% missing). These are summary statistics (kurtosis, skewness, etc.) only filled in on window-end rows, and are empty in the test set anyway.
3. Applied the same column selection to the test set.

```{r clean}
training <- training[, -(1:7)]
training <- training[, colMeans(is.na(training)) < 0.9]
training$classe <- factor(training$classe)

predictor_cols <- setdiff(names(training), "classe")
testing <- testing[, predictor_cols]

length(predictor_cols)
```

This leaves `r length(predictor_cols)` predictors and no missing values.

```{r classplot, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=5, fig.cap="Figure 1: Distribution of the classe outcome in the training data."}
barplot(table(training$classe), col = "steelblue",
        xlab = "classe", ylab = "Count")
```

The classes are reasonably balanced (A is somewhat more frequent), so plain accuracy is a fair metric.

## Model building

I split the training data 70/30 into a training set and a validation set. The validation set is never used for fitting or tuning, so it gives an honest estimate of out-of-sample error.

I chose a **random forest** because it handles many correlated numeric predictors, needs little preprocessing (no scaling required), captures non-linear interactions, and is known to work very well on this kind of sensor data.

**Cross-validation:** 5-fold CV inside the 70% training split, used to pick the `mtry` tuning parameter and to get a CV estimate of accuracy.

```{r model}
set.seed(123)
in_train <- createDataPartition(training$classe, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
trn <- training[in_train, ]
val <- training[-in_train, ]

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)

fit <- train(classe ~ ., data = trn, method = "rf",
             trControl = ctrl, ntree = 100)
fit
```

```{r cvplot, fig.height=3.5, fig.width=5, fig.cap="Figure 2: Cross-validated accuracy by number of predictors tried at each split (mtry)."}
plot(fit)
```

The best CV accuracy was **`r round(max(fit$results$Accuracy), 4)`** (mtry = `r fit$bestTune$mtry`).

## Out-of-sample error

```{r validate}
pred_val <- predict(fit, val)
cm <- confusionMatrix(pred_val, val$classe)
cm$table
cm$overall["Accuracy"]
```

Accuracy on the held-out validation set is **`r round(cm$overall["Accuracy"], 4)`**, so the **expected out-of-sample error is about `r round(1 - cm$overall["Accuracy"], 4)`** (`r round(100 * (1 - cm$overall["Accuracy"]), 2)`%). The cross-validation estimate (`r round(1 - max(fit$results$Accuracy), 4)` error) agrees closely with this, which suggests the model is not overfitting. The error on the final 20 test cases should be similar, with the caveat that 20 samples is a tiny sample, so the observed result can vary a lot by chance.

## Predictions for the 20 test cases

```{r predict}
test_pred <- predict(fit, testing)
data.frame(problem_id = 1:20, prediction = test_pred)
```

```{r write, eval=FALSE}
# Optional: write one file per prediction (not run during knit)
for (i in seq_along(test_pred)) {
  write.table(as.character(test_pred[i]),
              file = paste0("problem_id_", i, ".txt"),
              quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)
}
```

## Conclusion

A random forest with 5-fold cross-validation, trained on 52 sensor predictors after removing identifier and mostly-empty columns, achieved roughly 99% accuracy on held-out data. The expected out-of-sample error is under 1%, and this model was used to generate the predictions above for the quiz.
